title: True is His court
hookLine: true is the Lord, true His court, true His works (Sukhmani 17)

lines: CHANGE FOR A FIFTY, NOT A TWENTY.
cards: The cashier is busy and distracted, and she hands you change for a fifty when you gave her a twenty. Nobody saw. The store is a big chain; it won't miss thirty dollars.
You're halfway to the door. It's a small pause: the moment where the truth costs something and nobody would ever know. The seventeenth ashtpadi has an answer for that pause, and it isn't a rule.
It's a description of what the world is made of.

teach.h: SAT, SAT, SAT: LINE AFTER LINE.
teach.b: The first stanza of the seventeenth ashtpadi is built almost entirely out of one word, repeated: sat. True. In paraphrase: true are His feet, and true the one who touches them.
True His worship, true the one who serves. True His sight, true the one who sees. True His Name, true the one who remembers it.
True the Word, and true the One who speaks it. Line after line, sat, sat, sat, until truth isn't a single fact anymore but the material everything is made of.
Today's title adds an image from elsewhere in Gurbani: the dargah. Dargah is a Persian word for a royal court, where a ruler sits and cases are heard.

In Gurbani, the dargah is God's court, where every life is finally seen as it really was, and Gurbani calls it the sachee dargah, the true court. Not a court where the clever win, or the rich, or the well-connected.

teach.h: THE TRUE COURT, WHERE ONLY THE REAL COUNTS.
teach.b: A court where only what's real counts. Put those together and truth isn't one rule among many.

teach.h: TRUTH IS THE GRAIN OF THE WOOD.
teach.b: It's the grain of the wood. A lie isn't just breaking a rule; it cuts against the grain of everything. Read that way, the cashier moment changes.
The question stops being, will anyone know?
In the ashtpadi's picture of a world that's true all through, the thirty dollars is already known, not by a camera, but by the way things are. Handing it back isn't heroic. It's going with the grain.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi repeat sat, true, through line after line, and Gurbani speaks of the sachee dargah, God's true court, where each life is seen as it really was.

o: a judge's written ruling in a case
a court; in Gurbani, God's true court
a gate where pilgrims wash their feet

games.q: true is His court — tap the pairs.
p: true His feet, true who touches

s: dargah is a Persian word for a ruler's court
Gurbani uses it for God's court, where lives are seen truly.
in the true court, the clever and well-connected win
the seventeenth ashtpadi treats truth as one rule among many
sat runs through every line: truth is the grain of everything.

games.q: the cashier gave you change for a fifty instead of a twenty. nobody saw. what does the seventeenth ashtpadi suggest?
o: keep it; the chain won't notice.
hand it back: in a true world, it's already known.
games.why: the question stops being 'will anyone know?' if truth is the grain of everything, handing it back is simply going with the grain.

practice: Ask yourself one honest question, gently: is there one small place in my life where I've been a little untrue, an excuse, an exaggeration, a thing left unsaid? Don't judge it; just see it the way it really is.
Then picture the small true step, the correction, the plain answer, the change handed back, and rest with that picture.

wordCard.voice: Dargah, a court. The sachee dargah, where only what's real counts; in the seventeenth ashtpadi, everything about the One is sat, true, through and through.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dargah, a court; in Gurbani, God's court. From Persian.

carryVoice: Your line: true all through. Truth is the grain of the wood, not one rule among many. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 17, stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 285)
